title: Winterbourne Analytics - VPC scope and geo-gating discovery
summary: Initial networking intake for Winterbourne's private deployment. Discussed VPC peering vs PrivateLink/Private Endpoints, regional restrictions for EU data, egress IP allowlisting needs, transit gateway topology, and onboarding timeline. Agreed to a technical deep-dive and to exchange VPC diagrams and security docs.
topics: Egress IP and NAT / static IPs
next_steps: Josh to send SOC2 + security pack and private deployment checklist (by 2026-03-01)
Priya to schedule deep-dive with NetEng (week of 2026-03-08)
Customer to share VPC diagrams and current CIDR ranges (Tom/Aisha)
Agree pilot region (EU-WEST-1) and run connectivity test
action_items: Josh Carter: Share SOC2 report and private deployment checklist; due 2026-03-01
Priya Malhotra: Book 90m technical deep-dive with Diego and NetEng; target week of 2026-03-08
Tom Nguyen: Export and share VPC diagrams, peering routes, and outbound IP requirements; due 2026-03-02
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-25
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Josh Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Malhotra (Redwood SE), Evan Liu (Redwood SE), Tom Nguyen (Winterbourne CTO), Aisha Rahman (Head of Platform), Diego Silva (Network Engineer)

Summary/Notes: quick intake. rough audio, some words garbled.

[00:00] Josh Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Josh from Redwood Inference, i'll kick off. Can you hear me okay?
[00:08] Tom Nguyen: Yeah loud and clear, thanks Josh. Tom here. Appreciate the time.
[00:12] Aisha Rahman: Hi all, Aisha on the platform team. Diego's on for networking.
[00:16] Diego Silva: Hey.
[00:18] Priya Malhotra: Hi, Priya from solutions engineering, I'll be the technical lead on the deep-dive.
[00:23] Josh Carter: Great. Quick agenda: understand your current infra, geo gating / regs, egress needs, and then map onto Redwood's private options. also align on next steps. Sound ok?
[00:31] Tom Nguyen: Yep. We're evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private. For this call we want to scope private, because most of our inference traffic will touch EU personal data and we need strict residency and audit trails.
[00:43] Priya Malhotra: Understood. Can you describe your cloud footprint and where the workloads live?
[00:48] Aisha Rahman: Primary cloud is AWS. We have EU-WEST-1 for prod, US-EAST-1 for analytics, and APAC is experimental. For initial pilot we want EU only.
[00:59] Diego Silva: Our VPCs are managed per team. We use a transit gateway with hub-and-spoke for cross-account routing. We also have strict egress allowlists at the firewall level.
[01:10] Josh Carter: Ok. On Redwood Private we support VPC peering and AWS PrivateLink/private endpoints, and we can also integrate with transit gateway peering in many setups. Typical choices depend on whether you need provider-initiated connections or only customer-init... we — sorry, customer-initiated, right?
[01:28] Tom Nguyen: We prefer to control the peering side. Security team doesn't like provider side routing.
[01:33] Priya Malhotra: That's fine, we have both patterns. For customer-controlled peering we provide target endpoint information and you set up the peering and route table entries. For PrivateLink we provide an interface VPC endpoint that you create in your VPC and we manage the service side.
[01:47] Diego Silva: How do you handle egress IPs? We need static outbound IPs so downstream partners can allowlist.
[01:54] Evan Liu: For Private deployments we can provision NAT gateways or egress NAT through customer-managed transit. We can provide a set of egress IPs from the private dataplane or you can route through your NAT such that you own the egress IPs. If you want Redwood-owned static IPs, we can provision a fixed set in the hosted edges, but that's more common in Dedicated/Hosted.
[02:11] Diego Silva: Hmm, so if we keep egress in our VPC we keep control — that's preferred.
[02:15] Priya Malhotra: Yes, routing can be configured so customer owns outbound source IPs. We generally recommend customers own egress for strict allowlisting.
[02:23] Josh Carter: On region gating — you mentioned EU only for pilot. Two things — data plane (where inference runs) and control plane (management API/console). Do you require control plane to be in EU as well?
[02:36] Tom Nguyen: Ideally both. Our compliance team says admin metadata shouldn't leave EU. Is that something you can offer?
[02:43] Priya Malhotra: We do a private control plane option for Private deployments. It can be deployed in your account or a customer VPC in your region. We also support region-restricted control planes for enterprise contracts. We'll need to review exact compliance docs.
[02:55] Aisha Rahman: For keys — KMS — we require CMKs under our account.
[02:59] Evan Liu: That's supported. We can integrate with your KMS; you provide access with IAM roles and we don't hold plaintext keys.
[03:06] Diego Silva: Network ACLs — anything special on our end for conn tracking or health checks? Some vendors need a health check from their infra into our VPC and that's a no-go.
[03:15] Priya Malhotra: We try to avoid inbound checks into customer VPCs. Most integrations are initiated from within the customer's VPC (PrivateLink or peering) or via transit. If we need any health checks they can be outbound from your side to our endpoints. We'll document exact ports and CIDRs.
[03:29] Tom Nguyen: What about latency? Our product needs <60ms P95 for simple chat completions within EU. Will private reduce latency vs hosted?
[03:38] Josh Carter: Private in-region will generally give better predictability because you control networking. Dedicated in-region can be tuned for lower tail latency. Hosted can be low too but has multi-tenant variability. If you pin to an EU-only private deployment with local model runtime, you should meet the 60ms P95 for small models; larger context lengths will of course affect that.
[03:56] Diego Silva: Model sizes — we're evaluating smaller-medium models right now. Also testing KV cache behavior — we call it KV cash in our doc, lol.
[04:03] Priya Malhotra: (laughs) KV cache, yes. We'll share recommendations for sequence lengths and batching. Redwood Optimize can give you batching and cache config suggestions once we have a sample workload.
[04:13] Tom Nguyen: On security certifications — SOC2, ISO? Our compliance team will want the reports.
[04:20] Josh Carter: We'll send the SOC2 + ISO attestations. For Private deployments you also get audit logs shipped to your account and we support SAML SSO, RBAC, and integration with your SIEM.
[04:31] Aisha Rahman: Great. One concern — region availability windows. We sometimes have regulatory holds that require blocking certain regions, e.g., we cannot have data transit through specific countries. Can you support region-gating so traffic is pinned to eu-west-1 and never egress to other regions?
[04:45] Priya Malhotra: Yes, we can enforce routing policies in the control plane and data plane and define allowed regions. We'll need to validate with the operations team for truly enforced network-level guarantees; we'll add that as part of the deep-dive.
[04:57] Tom Nguyen: For peering, do you accept transitive routing across our transit gateway? We need to avoid route leaks between environments.
[05:05] Evan Liu: We can peer into a dedicated spoke VPC that you isolate; you can control route propagation so it's not transitive into other spokes. We typically recommend a dedicated Redwood service VPC per environment (prod/stage) to keep routes contained.
[05:18] Diego Silva: Anything on private DNS? We rely on private hosted zones and split-horizon DNS. Will Redwood endpoints resolve properly inside our VPC?
[05:26] Priya Malhotra: For PrivateLink the interface endpoints will use AWS private DNS names if you enable it; for peering you'll add A records pointing to the peered IP. We'll provide guidance for split-horizon and internal hostnames.
[05:37] Tom Nguyen: Ok sounds good. What about rollout? We plan a 3-week pilot in EU with a single model and a few routes.
[05:44] Josh Carter: Reasonable. Pilot checklist: VPC network diagram, egress plan (who owns NAT), KMS key setup, service accounts/roles, selected model image, and perf targets. We'll provide a checklist and the security pack.
[05:56] Aisha Rahman: One more question: if we want on-prem later, how much rework is expected? We have a few air-gapped locations for sensitive research.
[06:05] Priya Malhotra: On-prem is supported but it's a bigger engagement — air-gapped installs need additional ops work and there's an on-prem licensing path. We'll include high-level differences in the doc pack.
[06:15] Diego Silva: Any known gotchas with NACLs and UDP? We block a lot by default and only open minimal TCP.
[06:21] Evan Liu: Most of our control/data flows are TCP over TLS. We'll send a minimal port/port-range list. NACL statefulness can be tricky, but since we don't depend on UDP, it should be straightforward.
[06:33] Tom Nguyen: Good. Could you also run a quick network connectivity check — like a curl from our VPC to a staging endpoint — so we can validate routing?
[06:40] Josh Carter: Yes, we can spin up a staging endpoint in eu-west-1 and give you an endpoint and IPs for allowlisting. We'll need your egress plan and a contact to coordinate.
[06:48] Aisha Rahman: Diego will be the contact.
[06:50] Diego Silva: noted.
[06:51] Priya Malhotra: For the deep-dive, Diego, we want to walk through your transit gateway attachments and show a mock peering setup. Also we'll bring a network diagram with recommended route tables.
[07:03] Tom Nguyen: Timeline — what do you need from us to start the pilot?
[07:07] Josh Carter: VPC diagram, CIDRs, list of IPs allowed outbound, KMS key ARN, and a list of routes you'd like Redwood to have. We'll send the checklist by EOD.
[07:17] Aisha Rahman: Perfect. Anything else?
[07:19] Evan Liu: One note: if you later want Redwood-managed egress IPs for third-party allowlisting, there's an add-on, but since you control transit we'll keep it customer-owned to meet compliance.
[07:30] Tom Nguyen: Sounds good. Let's reconvene on the deep-dive next week.
[07:33] Josh Carter: Awesome. I'll follow up with the SOC2 packet, private deployment checklist, and propose slots for the deep-dive. Thanks everyone.
[07:39] Aisha Rahman: Thanks. Bye.
[07:41] Diego Silva: bye.

Meeting end.

Notes on quality: there were a few mis-transcribed phrases (KV cash, some names), and some timestamps approximate. The transcript keeps the conversational phrasing and includes action items and next steps as discussed.
